steps.label: Do Now: Question 2
steps.content:
Do Now: Marks on the Line

Think → Pair → ShareA sign says "50 or more". Why does the program use >= and not >?Show the answer

"Or more" includes 50 itself. > would leave out a mark of exactly 50.

3 minutes. What to do: from 3.1. The user types 45, 50, 72, 49, 50. Trace the program as it is written.

01  DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
02  DECLARE Index : INTEGER
03  DECLARE Count : INTEGER
04  Count ← 0
05  FOR Index ← 1 TO 5
06      INPUT Mark
07      IF Mark >= 50 THEN
08          Count ← Count + 1
09      ENDIF
10  NEXT Index
11  OUTPUT Count
Total: 2 marks

steps.label: Algorithms with Loops
steps.content:
Pseudocode and Software Development

Algorithms with Loops

Year 9, 3.2

  • Today: follow a loop in a flowchart and in pseudocode, and trace how the values change on every pass.
  • You already know: FOR loops, IF, and trace tables.
  • Activities: two trace tables, each harder than the last.
Think → Pair → ShareA flowchart has no FOR line. How could a flowchart still make steps repeat?Show the answer

An arrow can point back up to an earlier box. Then those boxes run again.

steps.content:
Watch a Flowchart Loop

Think → Pair → SharePredict before you start: how many times will the arrow go back up? Why?Show the answer

Three times. Count is 1, 2 and 3 when the answer is Yes. When Count is 4 the answer is No, so it leaves the loop.

5 minutes. What to do: press Next step. Before each press, say what happens next.

steps.label: Explain It: How a Flowchart Loops
steps.content:
Explain It: How a Flowchart Loops

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does Count have to change inside the loop?Show the answer

If Count never changed, the decision would give the same answer every time.

3 minutes. What to do: answer in your own words. Use Check my answer, improve it, then check again.

items.prompt: Explain how this flowchart repeats its steps, and how it knows when to stop. [2]
scheme: After the last box in the loop the arrow goes back (up) to the decision, so the boxes run again / repeat
The decision checks Count each time; while the answer is Yes it repeats, and when the answer is No (Count is more than 3 / Count is 4) it leaves the loop / stops
items.guidance: One mark for each point. Credit the ideas in the student's own words: an arrow or line going back (to the question / diamond / decision) for point 1; the question or decision answering No, or Count getting too big, for point 2. Do not accept "it loops" or "it repeats" alone for point 1.
items.context: The flowchart: Start, Total <- 0, Count <- 1, then a decision "Count <= 3?". Yes leads to Total <- Total + Count, then Count <- Count + 1, then an arrow back up to the decision. No leads to OUTPUT Total, then Stop. The class watched it run: Count was 1, 2 and 3 on the Yes passes, then 4 gave No and it output 6.
items.modelAnswer: After Count <- Count + 1 the arrow goes back up to the decision, so the boxes run again. When Count is 4, Count <= 3 is No, so it leaves the loop.

steps.content:
Check: Follow the Flowchart

Think → Pair → ShareA loop like this one has no Count ← Count + 1 box. Why would it never stop?Show the answer

Count would stay the same, so the decision would give the same answer every time.

4 minutes. What to do: follow the flowchart. Write a trace table in your book if it helps.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Compare: Flowchart and FOR Loop
steps.content:
Compare: Flowchart and FOR Loop

Think → Pair → SharePredict: do A and B output the same? Why does B have no line Count ← Count + 1?Show the worked answer

Both output 6. The FOR loop does the Count jobs for you.

A: flowchartB: FOR loop
Count ← 1FOR Count ← 1
Count <= 3?TO 3
Count ← Count + 1, arrow back upNEXT Count

A

B

01  DECLARE Total : INTEGER
02  DECLARE Count : INTEGER
03  Total ← 0
04  FOR Count ← 1 TO 3
05      Total ← Total + Count
06  NEXT Count
07  OUTPUT Total
  • FOR sets the start value, checks the last value and adds 1 at NEXT.
  • Same steps, same values, same output.

steps.label: Hinge Question: Match the FOR Line
steps.content:
Hinge Question: Match the FOR Line

Think → Pair → ShareWhy check the first value and the last value of Count separately?Show the answer

A loop can be wrong at either end. Checking both ends shows exactly which values of Count run the loop.

3 minutes. What to do: choose, then check.

items.prompt: Which FOR line does the same as this flowchart?
items.explain: Count starts at 2. The answer is Yes up to and including 6, because 6 <= 6 is TRUE. So 2 TO 6.

items.prompt: Another flowchart sets Count ← 1. Its decision is Count < 6? Which FOR line does the same?
items.explain: 6 < 6 is FALSE, so the last Yes pass is Count = 5. So 1 TO 5.

Activity 1: Trace Every Pass

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does this trace table have four values in the Output column, not one?Show the answer

The OUTPUT line is inside the loop, so it runs on every pass.

7 minutes. What to do: fill in the trace table, then check it. Done when every row is right.

steps.label: Check: A Loop with an IF
steps.content:
Check: A Loop with an IF

Think → Pair → ShareA loop runs 10 times and its IF is TRUE 4 times. Why does the line inside the IF run only 4 times?Show the answer

The loop reaches the IF on every pass, but the line inside it runs only when the condition is TRUE.

4 minutes. What to do: trace the loop. Check the IF line on every pass.

01  DECLARE Count : INTEGER
02  DECLARE Total : INTEGER
03  Total ← 0
04  FOR Count ← 1 TO 6
05      IF Count > 3 THEN
06          Total ← Total + Count
07      ENDIF
08  NEXT Count
09  OUTPUT Total
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Exam-Style Question: A Flowchart Loop
steps.content:
Exam-Style Question: A Flowchart Loop

Think → Pair → SharePart (a) has 2 marks. How do you plan the answer?Show the answer

Say what goes in and what comes out: one mark for each.

4 minutes. What to do: answer both parts in full sentences. Use Check my answer.

items.prompt: (a) State the purpose of this flowchart. [2]
scheme: It adds them up / finds the total and outputs the total
items.guidance: One mark for each point. Point 1 needs the number of inputs (5) or "five marks". Do not accept "it loops" or "it adds" alone.
items.modelAnswer: It inputs 5 marks and outputs their total.

items.prompt: (b) Explain why the box Count ← Count + 1 is needed. [2]
scheme: Count goes up by 1 on each pass / it counts how many marks have been input
So Count reaches 6 and the decision gives No, so the loop stops after 5 marks / without it the loop never stops
items.guidance: One mark for each point. Accept "so the loop ends" with a reason linked to Count for point 2. Do not accept "to add 1" alone.
items.modelAnswer: It adds 1 to Count on each pass. When Count reaches 6 the decision is No, so the loop stops.
